    • Technical indicator

    Stochastic RSI

    Stochastic RSI shows where RSI sits within its own recent values, on a 0 to 100 scale. Because it measures RSI rather than price, it moves much faster than RSI and reaches extreme values far more often. The common setting is 14/14/3/3; it is drawn as two lines called %K and %D.

    Which question does Stochastic RSI answer?

    Stochastic RSI answers this question: where is RSI between the lowest and highest of its last 14 values? If RSI is at the highest of its last 14 values the result is 100; at the lowest, 0.

    It is an "indicator of an indicator". Even if RSI makes small swings between 45 and 55, Stochastic RSI stretches that narrow range over 0–100, so it is far more volatile. Its quick response shows short-term changes early, but for the same reason it often swings between the extremes.

    How it is calculated

    1. Calculate RSI. The 14-period RSI is calculated as described on the RSI page.
    2. Find RSI's place in its last 14 values. Stochastic = (RSI − lowest of the last 14 RSI values) ÷ (highest − lowest) × 100.
    3. %K: a 3-candle average. The simple average of that value over the last 3 candles is the %K line; it smooths the raw value's jumps a little.
    4. %D: the average of %K. The simple average of %K over the last 3 candles is the %D line. %D trails %K slightly.

    How it is commonly read

    • Above 80 (upper zone): RSI is in the upper part of its last 14 values; momentum has leaned up over the last candles.
    • Below 20 (lower zone): RSI is in the lower part of its last 14 values; momentum has leaned down over the last candles.
    • %K crossing %D: %K crossing %D upward or downward describes that short-term momentum changed direction.
    • Staying at an extreme: in a strong trend Stochastic RSI can stay above 80 or below 20 for days.

    Because Stochastic RSI is calculated from RSI itself, it gives no information independent of it; it shows the same information on a faster, more volatile scale.

    Same scale, different context

    The extremes of Stochastic RSI mean different things depending on the structure of the market.

    Strong uptrend

    As RSI fluctuates in a high range, Stochastic RSI often touches 100. That describes a strong move; it does not say a fall is about to start.

    Strong downtrend

    Stochastic RSI can stay below 20 for a long time; being in the lower zone does not show that the fall is over.

    Sideways market

    When price moves back and forth in a range, Stochastic RSI swings quickly between the upper and lower zones; the extremes may line up more with the edges of the range.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • Where RSI sits within its last 14 values
    • The direction of short-term momentum and its changes, faster than RSI
    • Where %K and %D stand relative to each other

    What it does not prove

    • That price will fall above 80 or rise below 20
    • Information independent of RSI; it is derived from RSI
    • How long a move will last; being very fast, it changes direction often

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    Stochastic RSI gives no price level; it describes with what short-term momentum price arrives at a zone. Stochastic RSI in the lower zone as price approaches a support zone shows that declines have leaned over the last candles; whether the zone holds is still decided by the closes at the zone.

    Because it is a fast indicator, %K crossing %D together with a reaction at a zone is common. Both observations come from the same prices, so they do not confirm each other; reading them together only enriches the description.

    Stochastic RSI in crypto

    Crypto trades 24/7, so Stochastic RSI is calculated without interruption. On lower timeframes (such as 1H) it reaches the extremes very often; on higher timeframes (such as 1D) it swings less often but more meaningfully.

    Often confused with

    • RSI (Relative Strength Index)RSI measures changes in closing prices; Stochastic RSI measures where RSI sits within its recent values. That is why Stochastic RSI is much faster and more volatile.
    • MACDBoth are momentum indicators. Stochastic RSI is bounded between 0 and 100 and very fast; MACD is the difference of two averages, unbounded and slower.

    Key points

    • Stochastic RSI is where RSI sits within its last 14 values (0–100).
    • %K is the 3-candle average of that value; %D is the 3-candle average of %K.
    • It is much faster than RSI and reaches the extremes far more often.
    • Above 80 or below 20 does not mean a turn has to come.
